ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Gender based discrimination against SSC women officers in IAF  
*181. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether it is a fact that SSC women officers in IAF  are facing gender based discrimination which is 
affecting their service terms and conditions, whereas the similarly placed male SSC officers are being considered 
for permanent commission; 
(b)  if so, the action taken by the Ministry; and 
(c)  if not, the reasons for the delay? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE (SHRl M.M. PALLAM RAJU): (a) to (c) 
There is no discrimination between men and women with respect to the terms and conditions of service f or SSC 
officers in IAF as these are same for men and women SSC officers. The women SSC officers are eligible for similar 
pay and post retirement benefits akin to their male SSC counterparts. At present, Permanent Commission  is not 
being granted to any SSC officer, irrespective of gender.  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 181.  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, Question Nos. 181 and 188 are the same. Can we club them together?  
MR. CHAIRMAN: They are not quite the same. Let them be taken up separately. Now, estion No. 181, please.  
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Sir, my question relates to Short Service Commission, SSC, to officers in non-
combat posts like accounts, logistics, procurement of material, etc. The Minister has said that there is no 
discrimination, between male and female SSC officers. I would like to know from the hon. Minister, since 1993, how 
many male SSC officers have been given permanent commission and how many female SSC officers have been 
given permanent commission.  
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, the number of male SSC officers in the IAF, who were given permanent 
comission up to 2006 is 179. Subsequent to that, a view was taken, based on A.B. Singh Committee report that 
SSC officers will not be inducted into the permanent commission.  
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: How many female officers? Can you please inform?  
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: No female officers were inducted.  

2    Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: 179 male SSC officers were given permanent commission and not a single female 
SSC officer was given permanent comission. It shows , therefore, that the answer of the Minister that there is no 
discrimination in the IAF against women is completely false and it is proved by your own statement. Since there is a 
clear blatent discrimination, and we would not like  our defence services to be polluted by such gender  
discrimination, I would like to know from the hon. Minister, since he has admitted that not a single woman SSC 
officer has been given permanent commission, whether you are prepared to undo the discrimination that the women 
have faced and give them permanent commission, as their male .counterparts have been given.  
Thank you, Mr. Antony, I saw your statement on March 8 and I was happy to see that.  
SHRI A.K. ANTONY: Sir, as my colleague explained, at the moment, in the lAF's SSC officers, both men and 
women are on equal terms. Both are not allowed now. In the past it was there but after the A.V. Singh Committee 
report in 2006, the Government took a view. Not only the A.V. Singh Committee report, there was also a study by 
the headquarters of IDS. Then, the Government took a decision in 2006 that there would be no permanent  
commission for SSC officers, either for men or for women. That is the rule now.  
The problem is, in the services, the Government can not impose its decision. We have to consult the ser vice 
chiefs also. Unilaterally, the Government, whichever Government it is, does-not take decisions. But, I understand 
the sentiments of our women because, we are passing through an era of women empowerment in every field. We 
know, the trend all over the world is also changing. I can assure the Members that the Government will re-examine 
the decision, once again. We will try our best to find a solution to the long-pending demand of the women. We will 
try our best.  
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: Sir, the hon. Minister for Def ence is a very important 
Minister and very influential one. In spite of the lip service that we keep paying to the 
female gender and all the big things we say about t hem, Sir, the practical experience is that 
there is a hostile and venormous discrimination aga inst women in every department of the 
Government. There is discrimination at every place whether it is recruitment or any thing 
else. Sir, as we all know, we are the biggest users  of the Indian Airlines and Air India Planes. 
Sir, potbellied men with sloppy dresses go about in  cabin crew but a female who is one 
ounce more than the prescribed weight is grounded. What else is this if not discrimination? 
Will the hon. Minister give an assurance to the hou se that women will not be treated a? 
some kind of objects of sex or meant only to produc e aesthetic enjoyment for others and you ' 
will employ them and continue to employ them with c omplete equality? Will you examinal 
all the Departments of the Government and make an a ssurance to the House? ... 
(Interruptions)...   
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, I can speak for the Armed Forces and I can assure you of the highest degree of 
respect as far as women officers are concerned; and that will continue to be the ethos of the Armed Forces.  
SHRIMATI VIPLOVE THAKUR: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister when they recruited the Short 
Service Commission women whether it was written that they would not be given the Permanent Commission. Was 
this the condition while making them officers under the Short Service Commission? I want to know why they are not 
being taken as men are taken. If there is a condition I can understand that they were not taken. Secondly, because of 
the shortage of the officers in Air Force and in ail the other services - and they have said  

Oral Answers  [12 MARCH 2008]  to Questions   3 
that there is a Committee which has recommended that they would not be given a Permanent Commission—ar e they 
going to relax it and going to make the Short Service Commission as Permanent Commission?  
SHRl A.K. ANTONY: I have already assured the House when Brindaji asked her question. Even though under the 
present policy there is no Permanent Commission to the women, but as per the requests from various quarters mainly 
from women organisations and also Members of Parliament Unanimously, cutting across party lines, 1 ass ure the 
House that we will reexamine the case an we will try our best to find a solution.  
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. It is a general consensus of this House that though 
according to the law, as per the reply of the Minis ter and as per the presentation of the Minister, th ere is no 
discrimination, but the ground reality is that there is discrimination. That is how we look at it. In such situtation, what 
are all the measures that can be taken? How could you do that when in reality there is discrimination? Under the law, it 
may not be there.  
SHRI M.M. PALLAM RAJU: Sir, when the Short Service Commission was started, it was both for men and 
women and based on their ACRs, performance and base d on the needs, the Armed Forces did induct a few o f the 
men. Subsequently, in 2006, based on the recommendation of a Committee which was headed by the Headquarters of 
the Integrated Defence Staff, a decision was taken that no Short Service Commission officers either men or women 
would be taken into the Services. So. subsequent to that there is no question of any discrimination.

Possible dangers due to intrusion  
t*182. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
(a)  whether there is a decrease in the intrusion in var ious States by the foreign intruders on the various  
borders of the country during the last two years; 
(b)  the details of the possible dangers that might occu r from such intruders coming from the neighbouring 
countries; 
(c)  the measures taken by Government to curb such intrusion; 
(d)  the extent of effectiveness of these measures; and 
(e)  the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House.  
Statement  
(a) to (d) Available information about apprehension of foreign intruders, etc., indicates a decline in cross-border 
infiltration on the Indo-Pakistan and Indo-Bangladesh borders. There * is no significant incidence of cross-border 
intrusion of foreigners on the other borders. While illegal immigration into the country has various socio-economic 
implications, the dangers* from foreign infiltration relates mainly to their likely indulgence in subversive/terrorist , 
activities.  
(c) to (e) The Government have adopted a multi-pron ged approach to contain cross-border intrusions by 
foreign nationals which, inter-alia, includes round the clock surveillance & patrolling on the borders and 
establishment of observation posts; construction of border fencing and flood lighting; introduction of modern and 
hi-tech surveillance equipment; upgradation of intelligence set up and coordination with the State Governments and 
concerned intelligence agencies. As a result of these measures, cross-border intrusion has shown a declining trend.

♦183. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: W i l l  the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased 
to state:  
(/uni091A) whether investment in Research and Development in S cience and Technology in India remains 
below the required level as compared to the other developing countries; 
(/uni091B) whether Government proposes to liberalize Research and Development system to enhance scientific 
activities in the country; 
(/uni091C) whether Government has submitted any plan for Research and Development in Science and Technology to

Statement  
(a) Acording to the available official statistics, the expenditure on Research and Development (R & D)  as 
percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in India is lower compared to that of a few developing countries like 
Brazil and China, but it is higher compared to several developing countries like Argentina, Cuba, Sri Lanka and 
Paksitan as given in the Statement-I (See below)  

Oral Answers  [12 MARCH 2008]  to Questions   9 
 The Government has liberalised R & D  system to enhanc e scientific activities in the country in various 
ways. These include policy reforms, procedural reforms and organisational reforms such as formulation of S & T 
policies, setting up of autonomous research organisations and facilities in emerging and frontline are as, fiscal 
incentives and support measures to encourage investment on R & D in industry, national awards for outstanding 
R&D and encouraging public-private R&D partnerships. 
 and (d) Yes, Sir. The scientific Departments namely  Department of Science & Technology, 
Biotechnology, Scientific & Industrial Research, Atomic Energy, Space and Earth Sciences have submitted their 
plan proposal to the Planning Commission for XI plan allocations. The XI plan allocation for Scientific Departments 
has increased to Rs. 75,304,00 crores as compared t o Rs. 25,301,35 crores during X Plan as given in th e

SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Sir, my first supplementary is this. India has less then three take researchers in 
the field of science and technology whereas, our neighbouring country, China has more than nine lakh researchers 
in science and technology. Sir, in view of it, I would like to know from the hon. Minister the efforts made or proposed 
to be made to increase the number of researchers in science and technology.  
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am thankful to the hon. Member to have raised this issue. This is 
a matter that has exercised us for a period of time. Actually, the number of core researchers in this country is really 
not three lakhs or near that number. It is, in fact about 1.15 lakhs, and, as compared to China; China has about 8-10 
lakhs people in research. In fact, if you compare o ur people doing R&D in this country in comparison t o other 
countries in the world, you will find, the Scandinavian countries, for example, have a figure of about 7000 per million 
population; in the United States, it is about 4700 per million population, whereas, in India, it is 156.  
So, this is a very big issue and as far as the Gove rnment is concerned, the issue must be managed not only  
through greater investments by the public sector but also through more  

Oral Answers  [12 MARCH 2008]  to Questions    11  
investments in the private sector. The reality. Sir, is that as far as India is concerned invesment in  the R&D age 
percentage of GDP, is 0.8 per cent whereas in China, it is 1.23 per cent. In other countries of the world it is close to two 
or even three per cent, especially in the developed countries. But the component of the Government in this 0.8 per cent 
is 0.6 per cent, which is almost 80 per cent of the total investment in R&D. It is much more than that of any other 
country in the world. In China, the component of the public sector is close to 30 per cent. In the United States, it is 
about 30 per cent. In Japan, it is about 18 per cen t. So, the public sector component in R&D is much g reater in 
India than perhaps any other country in the world. But, unfortunately, the private sector component is  much less. 
So, as the private sector moves forward with liberalisation, and more money comes into the system, hopefully, the 
private sector component in R&D will increase. But as far as the Government is concerned. Sir, we are taking action in 
several areas. Firstly, in terms of tax incentives, the kind of incentives this Government has given has never been 
done before. For example, we now give a 150 per cent weighted deduction in the pharma sector, in the aeronautics 
sector, in the biotech sector, in the electronic sector and in several other sectors. We give a 125 per cent weighted 
deduction for sponsored research. Even for private companies now, as never before, we gave a 100 per cent deduction 
in both revenue and capital expenditure if it went into R&D. Companies can claim exemption from excise. They can 
claim exemption from customs duties. Let me just give you an example, Sir. In the pharma sector, earli er, when 
pharma companies used to go for clinical trials— ph ase-I and phase-II could be done in India—the expen diture 
made for Phase-Ill and Phase-IV outside India was n ot deductible. When our companies used to go outsid e for 
filing patents, which is a hugely expensive proposition, it was not deductible. But today, for example , under the 
Finance Act both activities are deductible. This has been done by this Government what has been done in the last 
three or four years, has never been done before in this country. We are now trying to improve the qual ity of 
researchers in this country. We are trying to set up two star colleges in every State. We are setting up centres of 
excellence in the university system. The problem is that in the last 25 years, our university stystem has expanded two-
and-a-half times, but research has not expanded. As far as national research laboratories are concerned, that number 
is. at least, static; it has not decreased. But the  university system has to be strengthened and we ar e trying very 
hard to do that.

Viability of SEZs in present economic scenario  
*185. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government has done any study or assessed the impact of the recent global economic slow down on 
the use and future of the numerous Special Economic Zones (SEZs) sanctioned in the country in the last two years;  

16    Oral Answers  [RAJYASABHA]  to Questions  
 whether it is a fact that the international economic slow down will impact the Indian exports; 
 if so, whether Government will do a rethink on the utility of SEZs in the near future; 
 whether it is also a fact that the targets of new units have fallen behind in SEZs; and 
 what steps are being proposed to review the viability of SEZs in the present economic climate? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL N ATH): (a) to (e) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House.  
Statement  
 No, Sir. 
 It is too early to conclude that the international economic slowdown could impact Indian exports. During 
the year 2006-07, exports from SEZs was of the order of Rs. 34,615 crore as compared to Rs. 22,840 crore in 2005-
06 and Rs. 18,314 crore in 2004-05, registering a g rowth of 89% in two years. In the current financial  year till 
December, 2007, exports have reached the level of Rs. 40,000 crore. 
 Special Economic Zones (SEZs) have brought in investments worth Rs. 70,225 in the new generation SEZs, 
out of which Rs. 67347 crore have been made in the SEZs notified under the SEZ Act, 2005. 
 No specific targets for new units in SEZs are set by the Government of India as these SEZs are set up by the 
private sector/State Government or private sector i n joint venture with State Government Agencies. As of date, 
Letters of Permission have been given for 177 units  in the newly notified SEZs which have already crea ted 
61015 jobs. 
 As the newly established SEZs are just getting esta blished/operational, it is too early to make any 
assessment on their viability which is constantly being evaluated by the Developers of SEZs and entrepreneurs in 
the manufacturing/service units who are investing their money.

picture of Special Economic Zones. In fact, the Indian rupee has been appreciating against dollar. The  value of 
dollar has been declining. This has created an adve rse impact on our exports. Our exporters have represented to 
the Government. The exporters of coir and other ind ustries, the exporters from Tirupur have represente d. Now, 
the Minister says that there is no impact; the global economic slow down has no impact. Is it true?  
I would like to ask the Minister: Do you say that the global economic slow down has no impact on our exports? 
Sir, the CAG report, which has been reported in the media, has made it very clear that the Special Economic Zone 
units have been achieving the prescribed net foreign exchange earnings mainly through domestic sales defeating one

in 200 select districts in the States with effect f rom 2.2.2006. The basic unit under NREGA 
is "household". During the year 2006-07, a total of  2.10 crore households had been provided 
employment under the Act in 200 districts. During t he current financial year, (up to mid- 
February, 2008), a total of 2.93 crore households i n 330 districts have been provided 
employment.  
(c) and (d) The Act is meant to provide wage employment to rural households that demand 
employment and are willing to do unskilled manual w ork. The workers are entitled to receive 
wages earned within 15 days of work done. In additi on, NREGA provides for workers 
entitlements during the course of work. These inclu de medical treatment (including 
hospitalization) at Government cost for injured wor kers for the injury acquired while working, 
ex-gratia payment to the legal heirs of the deceased or perma nently disabled workers by 
accident arising out of and in the course of employ ment, safe drinking water, shade for 
children and periods of rest, first aid box and cre che facility for children below 6 years of 
age of the female NREGA workers. The act also aims at creating durable assets and 
strengthening the livelihood resource base of the r ural poor. The choice of works suggested 
in the Act address causes of chronic poverty like d rought, deforestation, soil erosion, so that 
the process of employment generation is on a sustai nable basis. During the year 2006-07, a 
total of 830938 works had been taken up out of whic h 383491 works were completed during 
the year and the remaining 447447 works were in pro gress. During the current year, (up to 
January, 2008), 1370690 works have been taken up. O ut of these, 427531 works have been 
completed and 943159 works are in progress. Break u p of the works taken up under NREGA 
along with the benefits created during the year 200 6-07 and 2007-08 (up to January, 2008)

Disparity between farmers and rural workers  
*199. SHRI PRAVEEN RASHTRAPAL: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) the reasons for great economic divide between urban and rural India, inspite of 'Bharat Nirman' programme 
declared by Hon 'ble Prime Minister;  
* (b) the details of various programmes implemented through his Ministry to remove disparity of farmers and 
rural workers; and  
(c) whether Government has succeeded in stopping migration of workers from villages to towns due to National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Act (N.R.E.GA)?  
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) 
The Census of India 2001 indicates that opportunities in urban areas for employment, education etc. have been a pull 
factor attracting migration from rural to urban areas and from smaller towns and cities to larger urban areas. About 
98.3 million persons moved from rural areas to urba n areas during the last decade. Reasons cited for m igration 
over the last decade indicate that 14.4. million (1 4.7%) migrated for work/employment, 1.1 million (1. 2%) for 
business and 2.9 million (3%) for education. There is thus clear evidence of a rural-urban divide which indicates 
the need fogenerating rural employment, enhancing rural prosperity and providing rural educational and  health 
facilities to achieve balanced socio- economic grow th. Lack of infrastructure, such as rural road, ele ctricity, 
drinking water etc., is a major reason for the rural-urban divide.  
To address these, Bharat Nirman is announced by the  Government as a time bound plan for development of  
rural infrastructure to be implemented over a period of four years i.e. 2005-06 to 2008-09 with the total estimated 
investment of Rs. 1,74,000 crore comprises six comp onents i.e. Irrigation, Rural Roads, Rural Housing, Rural 
Drinking Water Supply, Rural Electrification and Telephone Connectivity. Three of the six components namely, Rural 
Roads, Rural Housing and Rural Drinking Water Suppl y are being implemented by the Ministry of Rural 
Development with an estimated investment of Rs. 85.000 crore. These components have well defined targets and 
the progress is closely monitored.  

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions   37  
The other programmes implemented by the Ministry of  Rural Development are Swarnjayanti Gram 
Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) to provide self employment,  while the Sampooma Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) 
aims at providing additional wage employment in rural areas there by providing food security and improved nutrition, 
and creation of durable community assets and infrastructure. The SGRY is being subsumed under the National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Scheme. Total Sanitation Campa ign (TSC) aims at development of rural sanitarian 
infrastructure and their use. Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP) an J National Programme for 
Comprehensive Land Resource Management (NPCLRM) are implemented for area development.  
The Provision of Urban Amenities in Rural Areas (PURA) Scheme was implemented on a pilot basis on seven 
targeted areas in States to provide physical and social infrastructure in the identified rural clusters to further their 
growth potentials.  
(c) the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NR EGA) has been implemented in 330 districts of the 
country and would be extended to the remaining districts w.e.f. 1st April, 2008. The objective is to ensure that local 
employment is provided to every willing rural house hold for at least 100 days of unskilled manual work s in a 
financial year and in the process it would result i n building durable assets, strengthening of livelihood resource 
base of rural population. During 2006-07, 90.51 cro re persondays and during 2007-08 (upto February, 20 38) 
111.38 crore persondays of employment were generated. It is expected that with the implementation of NREGA in all 
the districts, the migration of workers from villages to towns would reduce.

Sir,  
1 am directed to convey the sanction of the Government of India to a Study to be assigned to the Indian Council 
for Research on International Economic Relations (I CRIER) on the Impact of organized retailing on the 
unorganized retail sector.  
Objective of the Study : 
2. There has been considerable growth in organized retailing in the country in recent years and estima tes 
show a much faster growth in the future. Major indu strial houses have entered this area and have announced the 
future expansion plans. Transnational corporations are also seeking to come to India and set up retail  chains in 
collaboration with Indian big companies, Divergent views have been expressed on the impact of the growth in the 
organized retail in the country. Concerns have been  raised that the growth of organized retailing may have an 
adverse impact on the retailers in the unorganized sector. It has also been argued that growth of organised retailing will 
yield efficiencies in intermediary stages enabling higher prices or access to markets to producers (in cluding 
farmers or small producers) or lower prices to consumers. To reconcile such variations, an in-depth analytical study 
on the possible effects of organized retailing in India is essential.

Terms of Reference  
3. In order to assess the impact of growing organiz ed retail on different aspects of the economy, ICRI ER is 
appointed to carry out a study on organized retail focused on the following:  
(i) Effect on small retailers and vendors in the unorganized sector keeping in mind the likely growth in the 
overall market.  
(ii)  Effect on employment  
(iii)  Impact on consumers  
(iv)  Impact on farmers and manufacturers  
(v)  Impact on prices  
(vi)  Overall impact on economic growth  
ICRIER will analyse the above in the context of a g rowth scenario of 7-10 per cent per annum in the ne xt 5 
years and in the light of practice in other fast growing emerging market economies.

4. The study by ICRIER will involve the following:  
 Literature survey of existing studies 
 4-5 case studies of established retail chains 
 Interviews of major players in the organized retailing, manufacturers, and of producers including 
associations of farmers. 
 Questionnnaire-based survey of unorganized retailers, including vendors especially around organized 
retail shops 
• Questionnaire-based survey of consumers around th e organized retail outlets

1258. DR. K. MALAISAMY: 
SHRI S. ANBALAGAN:

 in the Free Trade Agreement between India and China in the recent past what are the major gains that India

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) In pursuance to the recommendation of JSQ a Joint Task 
Force to study in detail the feasibility of India-China RTA was set up. The JTF has finalized its report in its last 
meeting held in October, 2007. According to the JTF report, India-China RTA would be mutually advantageous. It 
will promote economic growth, enhance welfare gains and increase bilateral trade through efficient allocation of

services. In sectors like textile and chemicals. China and India share similar industrial structure, and there is scope

sensitive products may need to be excluded from tariff liberalization.

Scrapping of import duty on items from neighbouring countries  
1260. SHRI D. RAJA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that Government had scrapped i mport duty on more than 4800 items from four 
neighbouring countries and reduced customs tariff on these products from Pakistan and Sri Lanka as part of the 
efforts to boost trade in South Asia; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether Government are aware that this step will affect the indigenous producers of these commodities 
adversely, particularly cash crop producers in Kerala; and 
 if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) India is one of the signatories to the Agreement on South 
Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) which came into force from 1st January, 2006 and became operational from 1st 
July, 2006. As per the Article 7 of the Agreement scheduled for Phased Trade Liberalization Programme (TLP) 
has been stipulated according to which:  
(i) India, as non-member of SAFTA would reduce tariff for other non-LDCs members, namely; Pakistan and 
Sri Lanka to 20% by 31.1.2007 and thereafter to 0—5% in the next five years i.e. by 31.12.2012.  
(ii) Non-LDC members would reduce tariff to 0—5% fo r LDC members within 3 years of coming into 
force of SAFTA Agreement i.e. by 31.12.2008.  
(iii) The Article also stipulates that the schedules of tariff reductions would not prevent any contracting State 
from immediately reducing from tariff to 0—5% or fr om following an accelerated schedule to tariff 
reduction.  
During the 14th SAARC Summit held in New Delhi, Ind ia had announced unilateral acceleration of tariff 
reduction in order to provide greater market access to the least developing country Members of SAARC. In pursuance 
of this announcement India has unilaterally notified reduction to tariff to zero for LDC members of SAFTA w.e.f. 
1.1.2008 thereby advancing the stipulated period by one year. The beneficiaries of these unilateral reductions are 
LDC- Members namely; Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives and Nepal. The accelerated tariff reductions, therefore, are 
not available to exports coming from Pakistan and Sri Lanka.  
(c) and (d) In order to protect the interest of the domestic producers, each Member State of SAFTA has kept 
Sensitive List (s) and the items in the Sensitive Lists are excluded from SAFTA tariff concessions. India has kept 
two Sensitive Lists, one with 865 items for Non-LDC members and another with 744 items for LDC members, and 
most of th,e cash crops products are included in the Sensitive Lists of India.

Utilization of offset amount  
1273. SHRIKALRAJMISHRA:  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:  
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state:  
 the details of the offset clause in the recent Defence Procurement Procedures (DPP) 2006; 
 whether Government has formulated guidelines regarding utilization of such offset amount; 
 whether Government has constituted any nodal group in the Ministry to channelise the offset amount; 
and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A. K. ANTONY): (a) to  (d) Government promulgated Defence 
Procurement Procedure (DPP) 2006 with effect from 1st September, 2006 to ensure expeditious procurement of the 
approved requirements of the Armed Forces in terms of capabilities south and time frame prescribed. Procedure for 
implementing Offset  

62    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
Provisions is part of DPP-2006. Offset clause is applicable for all procurement proposals where indicative cost is 
Rs. 300 crore or more and the schemes are categoriz ed as 'Buy (Global)' involving outright purchase fr om 
foreign/Indian vendors and 'Buy and Make with Transfer of Technology' i.e. Purchase from foreign vendor follwed 
by licensed Production. A uniform offset of 30% of the indicative cost of the acquisition in 'Buy (Global)' category 
acquisitions and 30% of the foreign exchange compon ent in 'Buy and Make' category acquisitions will be  
minimum required value of the offset. The Defence Acquisition Council may, after due deliberations, also prescribe 
varying offset percentages above 30% for different classes of cases or for individual cases depending upon the factors 
involved such as strategic importance of the acquisition or technology, enhanced ability of Indian defence industry 
to absorb the offset, export potential generated et c. Offset obligations are to be discharged directly  by any 
combination of the following methods:  
(i) Direct purchase of, or executing export orders- for defence products and components manufactured 
by, or services provided by, Indian defence industries, i.e. Defence Public Sector Undertakings, the 
Ordnance Factory Board, and any private defence ind ustry manufacturing these products or 
components under an industrial licence granted for such manufacture. For the purpose of defence offset, 
"services" will mean maintenance, overhaul, upgrada tion, life extension, engineering, design, 
testing, defence related software or quality assurance services.  
(ii) Direct foreign investment in Indian defence in dustries for industrial infrastructure for services, co-
development, joint ventures and co-production of defence products.  
(iii) Direct foreign investment in Indian organizat ions engaged in research in Defence Research & 
Development as certified by Defence Offset Facilitation Agency (DOFA).  
Government has constituted Defence Offset Facilitation Agency (DOFA) with a charter to:— 
 Facilitate implementation of the offsets policy. 
 Assist in vetting of offset proposals technically. 
 Assist in monitoring the offset provisions. 
 Suggest improvements in the policy and procedures. 
 Interact with Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff and Service Headquarters. 
 Advise, in consultation with the Headquarters Integ rated Defence Staff, Services and Defence 
Research and Development Organization, areas in which offsets will be preferred. 
 Promote exports of defence products and services. 
(h) Provide advisory clarifications on the policy and procedures.  
Vacancies in the armed forces  
1274. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state:  
(a) the details of vacancies at present in the armed forces;  

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions   63  
 since when these vacancies have been in existence; 
 whether these vacancies have been advertised and given wide publicity; 
 if so, what has been the response; 
 whether it is a fact that the response to advertisements, opinion polls and the process of admission in defence 
establishments reveals that the youth are not inclined to come forward to take army as a carrier; and 
 the steps Government is contemplating to address the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A. K. ANTONY): (a) to (f) There is a shortage of 11,153,1403 and 
1368 officers in Army Navy and Air Force respectively. This deficiency has been continuing since very long time in 
varying degree. There is no shortage of Personnel Below Officer Ranks (PBOR) in the Armed Forces.  
The Armed Forces have undertaken sustained image projection and publicity campaign to create awareness 
among the youth on the advantages of taking up a ch allenging and satisfying career. Candidate-friendly  
recruitment procedures to attract more number of candidates and a focused publicity drive in various institutions to 
attract potential candidates have been undertaken. Awareness campaigns, participation in carreer fairs  and 
exhibitions, advertisements in print and electronic media, counselling and motivational talks in schools, colleges and 
NCC camps are also some of the other measures in this direction. In addition, the commitment and bravery of the 
Armed Forces is consistently projected through the electronic and print media.  
There has been adequate response to the advertiseme nts for joining the Armed Forces. Although a good 
number of candidates pass through the written part of the examination, many fail to make the grade at the stage of 
Service Selection Board (SSB) interviews, which is mandatory for selection of officers, as they are not able to meet 
the requisite selection and medical criterion.  
The shortfall in recruitment of officers in the Defence Services are largely due to change in the socio-economic 
environment and the resultant changes in career preferences, better employment opportunities in other sectors, tough 
selection procedures and service conditions required for the Defence Forces.  
Several steps have been taken by the three Services to attract more talented youth to join the Defence Forces. 
All officers including those in Short Service Commission (SSC) have been made eligible to hold substantive rank 
of Captain, Major and Lieutenant Colonel after 2, 6 and 13 years of reckonable service respectively. In addition to 
the above, 750 posts of Lieutenant Colonels have been upgraded to Colonel's rank. The tenure of SSC officers has 
also been extended from 10 years to 14 years.  
The Government has also appointed Sixth Central Pay Commission to go into the question of revision of pay and 
allowances etc. of all the Government servants including the Armed Forces. The three Services have presented a 
joint memorandum to the Pay Commission suggesting revision of pay and allowances and other service conditions. 
The matter has also been discussed with the Pay Com mission by the three Service Chiefs and officers in  the 
Ministry of Defence.

Increase in temperature of Arctic Ocean  
1280. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of EART H SCIENCES be pleased to 
state:  
(a) whether Government is aware that the temperature of Arctic Ocean has been increasing rapidly;  

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions   67  
 if so, the details thereof received by Government; 
 how much water level of the ocean has increased during the last 10 years, year-wise; 
 how far Indian coast shall be adversely affected as a result of such increase of water-level; and 
(e) the steps being taken/taken by Government for the protection/safety of India? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir.  
 The information available in published reports indicate that the sea surface temperatures (SST) and the upper 
ocean heat content in the Arctic Ocean have been st eadily increasing. Few climate stations that have r ecords 
extending back beyond 50 years, indicate that the A rctic region warmed up by about 1-2°C between 1910 and 
1945. A number of stations showed further warming o ver the past two decades. The SST recorded in 2007,  is 
reported to have been about 3.5°C warmer than the 100 year average. 
 The average volume of Arctic Ice is 20,000 Km 3, compared to the Antarctic Ice volume (30,000,000 
Km 3). Since the quantity of ice in Arctic is very smal l compared to Antarctic, Arctic sea ice melting doe s not 
increase the water level of the oceans significantly. 
 Since melting of the ice cover on the Arctic Ocean does not affect sea level significantly, the coastal areas will 
not be adversely affected. 
 Government has set up a network of about 50 tidal g auges all along Indian coast line for continuous 
monitoring of sea level. Besides, Coastal Zone vuln erability zonation maps are being generated for var ious 
sectors along the Indian Coast.

Coastal Security Scheme for Gujarat  
1283. SHRI KESHUBHAI S. PATEL: SHRI JAYANTILAL 
BAROT: SHRI SURENDRA MOTILAL PATEL:  
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
 whether Government of Gujarat has submitted any proposal for Coastal Security Scheme; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): 
(a) Yes, Sir.  
(b) A comprehensive Coastal Security Scheme, which is under implementation since 2005-06 over a period  
of 5 years, was formulated after consultations with  all agencies concerned as well as all the 9 coasta l States 
including Gujarat and 4 Union Territories. Based on  the proposal of State Government of Gujarat, the C oastal

five years and any such proposal could be considered only at the time of review after that.

Guides of naxalism in Andhra Pradesh  
t l284. SHRl SHREEGOPAL VYAS: MISS 
ANUSUIYA UIKEY:  
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that the main guides of naxalism are in Andhra Pradesh; 
 if so, the advice Centre is giving to the State to bring them into mainstream; and 
 whether Centre has given suitable directions to the  concerned States to check the entry of specially 
trained naxalites in Chhattisgarh from neighbouring States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAI RS (SHRI SHRIPRAKASH 
JAISWAL): (a) to (c) Several naxal outfits under di fferent names are operating at present, with leader s from 
various States, including Andhra Pradesh.  
Law and order being a State subject, action with respect to various aspects/issues related to naxalite activities 
lies primarily in the domain of the concerned State Governments. The Central Government, however, supplements 
their efforts and resources by a variety of measure s that include deployment of Central paramilitary forces which 
work under the control of the State Government concerned, sanctioning of India Reserve battalions, assistance for 
strengthening of the State police and Intelligence agencies, re-imbursement of security-related expenditure, assistance in 
training of State police forces, sharing of Intelli gence, facilitating inter-State coordination and as sistance in 
development works through a range of schemes of various Ministries.  
Some naxalite affected States have their own State-specific surrender and rehabilitation policies for naxalites, 
which are implemented by the State Governments conc erned. Under the Security Related Expenditure (SRE)  
Scheme of Government of India, security-related expenditure is reimbursed to naxalite affected States for various 
items, which include reimbursement of expenditure u pto Rs. 10,000 for a surrenderee without arms and u pto 
Rs. 20,000 for a surrenderee with regular weapons i n respect of hardcore, underground naxalite cadres and 
members of dalams who surrender in accordance with the surrender and rehabilitation policy being implemented by 
the concerned State Government.  
State Governments conduct need-based inter-State joint police operations. A Task Force under Special Secretary 
(Internal Security), consisting of officers of inte lligence agencies, State police forces and Central paramilitary 
forces, deliberates upon the gamut of operational s teps needed to deal with the naxalite activities an d facilitates 
coordination between authorities of different States as may be necessary.

PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA:  « 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:  
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government has recently decided to undertake a comprehensive review of  the 
Coastal Security Scheme in view of illegal cross border activities;  
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether the coastline along several States and Union Territories are prone to illegal cross border activities 
including smuggling of explosives; and 
 if so, to what extent comprehensive review of coastal security scheme is going to curb illegal cross border 
activities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): (a) 
and (b) No, Sir. The review of the implementation of the Coastal Security Scheme is done time-to time to monitor 
the physical progress of implementation of the Scheme. A review meeting of the Coastal Security Scheme (CSS) under 
the Chairmanship of Union Home Secretary was recently held on 13.12.2007.  
Various issues such as physical progress of activities, manpower, jurisdictional issue, hiring of boats etc. were 
discussed in the meeting. It was decided that each State will prepare a detailed action plan setting time lines for the 
activities of these various issues under the Scheme.  
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The inputs from various agencies suggest that several States & UTs  j 
are prone to cross border illegal activities. Concerned State authorities and field formations are sensitized as and 
when such inputs are received. The periodic comprehensive review of implementation of the Scheme fine-tunes the 
process of implementation of the Scheme, which aims to curb illegal cross border activities through coastal areas 
of the country.

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    107  
Maoist of Nepal intruding bordering area of Uttarakhand  
tl313. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
 whether it is a fact that Maoist of Nepal are intruding in the bordering areas of Uttarakhand and they have 
also damaged Indian property there; 
 whether Government is taking any concrete steps for its border security to curb such incidents in futu re; 
and 
 whether Government has made contact with Government of Nepal officially in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V RADHIKA SELVI): 
(a) India-Nepal have open border and visa free regi me. There are no restrictions on the movement of bo th 
nationals across the border. There are no reports c onfirming any intrusion of Maoist of Nepal in the b ordering 
areas of Uttarakhand and damage to Indian property.  However, because of internal situation in Nepal, s ome 
significant activities of Maoist have been reported in areas of Nepal bordering India.  
 Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) which is the Border Guard ing Force on the India-Nepal border maintains a 
constant vigil to check any hostile activity. SSB has also been asked to work in close coordination with the State 
Governments having border with Nepal to check the e ntry of undesirable elements into India. Government  of 
India is also keeping a close watch on overall situation. 
 India and Nepal have various bilateral mechanisms to address issues of mutual security concern including 
entry of undesirable elements into each others territory. 
Steps to examine various natural calamities in Kerala  
1314. SHRI P.R. RAJAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government has taken any step during th e last one year to examine various 
natural calamities in Kerala;  
(b) if so, the details including the reasons identi fied and loss due to land slides, 
land slip coastal erosion and flood that have accrued in various districts during last one  
year;  
 the steps taken to provide assistance to the State so as to recover from calamities during the last on e 
year; and 
 the details of short term steps adopted to control above natural calamities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): (a) 
to (d) As per the information furnished by the Government of Kerala, the Geological Survey of India and the Centre for 
Earth Science Studies have been monitoring the various natural calamities in the State. During the last one year, the 
Geological Survey of India has studied 42 landslide s / debris flow / land slump incidents in Idukki, P alakkad, 
Malappuram, Kozhikkode, Wayanad and Kannur Districts of Kerala and has assessed the causative factors besides 
suggesting mitigative, remedial and control & corrective measures

for implementation by the local authorities. In add ition, the Geological Survey of India has, in its a nnual 
programmes for 2006-07 and 2007-08 included detaile d site-specific mesozonation studies of landslide p rone 
areas in Erattupetta (Kurisumala) and Munnar in Idukki district and also preparation of landslide inventory of the 
State as a whole. A few more places like Amboori area in Thiruvanathapuram district and in Wayanadu, Kannur and 
Kozhikode districts have been identified for the Feasibility Study Programme. Rapid survey of the.landslide sites 
were conducted during June-July-August 2007 in the aforesaid districts.  
Centre for Earth Science Studies (CESS), has taken up research programmes on various hazards on long term 
basis and they have prepared landslide and hazard z onation maps of Kollam District and some areas of

with the support of Ministry of Earth Science. Reco nnaissance studies were conducted by UT Chennai on the 
extent of and remedial measures against coastal erosion in the State and steps are already taken to im plement its

As per information received from the State Governme nt, during the year 2007-08 all the 14 districts we re

As per the existing scheme for financing the relief expenditure, the State Government concerned is required to 
undertake immediate relief operations out of the co rpus of Calamity Relief Fund, which is contributed by the 
Government of India and the State Government in the ratio of 3:1. Additional financial assistance is also provided 
to the affected States in the wake of calamities of  severe nature from National Calamity Contingency F und 
(NCCF), after following the laid down procedure.  
During 2007-08, an amount of Rs. 94.26 crore has been allocated in the CRF of Kerala consisting of Rs.70.70 
crore as Central contribution and Rs.23.56 crore as State contribution. The Government of India have released the

2007.

works wherever required.

of schemes of various Ministries, including various income-generating, public-utility and social-security schemes of 
Ministries like Rural Development, Agriculture, Youth Affairs and Sports, Panchayati Raj and Tribal Affairs.  
33 battalions of Central paramilitary forces (inclu siving of 1 battalion of State Armed Police on inte r-State

Protection from external aggression after IMDT Act  
1328. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: 
SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI:  
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether, on July 14,2005, Supreme Court in Writ Petition No. 131/2000 in the matter  

118    Written Answers to  [RAJYASABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
of Sarbanand Sonwal Vs. Union of India, held that the illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1998 and 
the rules made thereunder, are ultra vires and struck it down and observed that the centre had not done its duty to 
protect Assam from 'external aggression';  
 Government's evaluation of magnitude/threat perception of such aggression; 
 who are responsible and who constitute this aggression; and 
 the steps taken by Government to protect Assam from so called 'external aggression'? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): 
(a) The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India vide its judgement dated 12.7.2005 in Writ Petition No. 131/2000 in the 
matter of Sarbanand Sonowal Vs. Union of India, held that the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 
1983 and the Rules made thereunder, are ultra vires  and struck it down. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, inter alia, 
directed that all cases shall be decided in the man ner provided in the Foreigners Act, the Rules made thereunder 
and the procedure prescribed under the Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964. The Government was also directed to 
constitute sufficient number of Tribunals under the Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964, to effectively  deal with 
cases of foreigners, who have illegally come from Bangladesh or are illegally residing in Assam.  
(b) to (c) The Government is aware of illegal immigration/infiltration from Bangladesh into various parts of the 
country. However, as this activity takes place clandestinely, no specific details are available about the magnitude 
of this illegal infiltration.  
(d) The Government has taken up various measures to curb illegal influx into the country, which inter alia includes 
strengthening of Border Security Force (BSF) and eq uipping them with modern and sophisticated 
equipments/gadgets; reduction of gaps between borde r outposts, intensification of patrolling, accelera ted 
programme of construction of border roads and border fencing etc. The State Governments/UT Administration have 
been empowered under section 3(2) (c) of the Foreigners Act, 1946 to detect and deport foreign nationals illegally 
staying in India. Administrative instructions are issued from time to time requesting the State Govern ments/UT 
Administration to detect and deport illegal Bangladeshi migrants staying in the country. In addition, thirty-two (32) 
foreigners tribunals under the provisions of Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964 have been constituted in the State of 
Assam for detection of illegal migrants/foreigners.

 the losses suffered by Rajasthan due to floods duri ng August 2006, amounts to relief requested from

 the measures Government intend to take to check endemic flood menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V.

RADHIKA SELVI): (a) to (d) The details of damage du e to flash floods/floods/landslides/ cloudburst etc ., as 
reported by the States/Union Territories during the last five years, are enclosed as Statement-I (See below).  
State Governments are primarily responsible to take  rescue and relief measures in the wake of natural 
calamities. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Governments by providing financial and 
logistic support, where necessary. To ensure ready availability of funds with the States to undertake immediate 
rescue and relief operations in the wake of natural calamities, a Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) has been constituted 
with an allocated amount for each State, which is contributed by the Government of India and the concerned State 
Governments in the ratio of 3:1. For calamity of a severe nature, additional financial asistance is also considered from 
the National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), after following the laid down procedure.  
Details of the funds released to the States from CR F and NCCF during the last five years is enclosed a s 
Statement-II.  
The Government of Rajasthan, in their memorandum, s ought financial assistance of Rs. 3248.22 crore for  
management of floods during August, 2006.  
Keeping in view the magnitude of the situation, the Government of India had released on 6th September, 2006, 
an amount of Rs. 350.00 crore, as per details given  below, to enable the Government of Rajasthan to undertake 
rescue and relief operations in the affected areas: 
(i) Rs. 163.66 crore as advance release of second instalment of Central share of Calamity Relief Fund 
(CRF) for the year 2006-07.  
(ii) Rs. 86.34 crore as advance release of 25% of the Central share of CRF for the year 2007-08.  
(iii) Rs. 100.00 crore as 'on account' release from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF).  
The 1st instalment of Central share of CRF for the year 2006-07 amounting to Rs. 163.66-crore was earl ier 
released on 28th June, 2006.  
The request of the Government of Rajasthan for addi tional Central assistance was considered by the Hig h 
Level Committee which had approved the following assistance:—  
(i) Rs. 240.44 crore from NCCF subject to adjustment of 75% of the balance available in the CRF 
account of the State for the instant calamity.  
(ii) Rs. 5.00 crore from Special Component of Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP).  
(iii) Release of 60400 MT foodgrains for relief employment from the Special Component of Sampoorna 
Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY).  
Flood Management being a State subject, the schemes  for flood control are planned, funded and executed by 
the State Governments. The role of Central Government is technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. However, 
Government of India is providing Central assistance  to State Governments to carry out flood control an d river 
management works, in the critial reaches.  
A State sector scheme proposed by the Ministry of W ater Resources, namely "National Flood Management 
Programmes" with an outlay of Rs. 8000/- crore has been approved by the Government in principle, in 
November, 2007 for providing Central assistance to the State Government during XI Plan period (2007-12 ). It 
covers the critical flood management and erosion control works taken up by the States.

and (b) 17 fatal attacks on senior citizens took place during 2007 in comparison to 12 attacks in the year 2006. The 
steps taken by Delhi Police for security of senior citizens include establishment of helpline; identification of elderly 
people living alone, verification of antecedents of  their employees, particularly domestic servants an d drivers; 
periodic visits to the residence of elderly persons by the Beat Staff and Station House Officers; setting up of Sentior 
Citizen's Security Cell; contacting the senior citi zens by the officers of the Senior Citizen Security  Cell, both 
personally and on telephone to give them emotional support and to create a sense of security; briefing the senior 
citizens about security devices and security relate d issues; adoption of senior citizens by school chi ldren; and 
organizing security awareness camps for the benefits of senior citizens, starting community liaison programme to 
involve senior citizens in larger community matters, distribution of printed material on the steps to be taken for the 
safety of life and property of senior citizens, educating senior citizens regarding law related to the ir safety and 
welfare, etc.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND  EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR 
FERNANDES): (a) As per National Sample Survey Organisation 61 st round Survey Report-2004-05, unemployment

inter alia, indicated working poverty rates for South Asia, which includes India, were 33% for US$ 1 a day and 80.3%

mainly the result of the continuing low levels of productivity.

and (b) Under the Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986, employment of children is prohibited in 15 occupations

1352. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state:  
 whether the National Commission for Enterprises - in the Unorganized Sector has informed that 77 per cent of the 
unorganized workers are living in abysmal conditions and under poverty; 
 whether this Commission also suggested the creation of the National Fund for Unorganized Sector (NAFUS); 
and 
 if so, the details of decisions and actions proposed by Government to save such huge percentage of unorganized 
population? 
THE MI NI STER OF  STATE OF  THE MI NI STRY OF  LA BOUR A ND EMPL OYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) As 
per the Report given by the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganized Sector (NCEUS), at the end of 2004-05, about 836 
million or 77% of the population were living below Rs. 20/- per day. However, the poverty figures  

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    141  
that have been mentioned stop at 2004-05. Therefore, the report can not be seen as a reflection of the policies pursued 
in the recent past.  
(b) and (c) The NCEUS has recommended creation of National Fund for Unorganised Sector. However, this 
recommendation was not accepted as it was felt that  in view of the varied nature of the schemes, the s ource of 
funding should by prescribed in the schemes themsel ves. The Government has introduced the Unorganised Sector 
Workers' Social Security Bill, 2007 in Rajya Sabha on 10.09.2007.  
The 'Rashtriya Swasthya BimaYojana' for BPL families in Unorganised Sector has been launched on 1st October, 
2007. The unorganized sector worker and his family (unit of five) will be covered under the scheme. The total sum 
insured would be Rs. 30,000/- per family per annum on a family floater basis. The benefits under the scheme will 
start accruing from 1st April, 2008.  
With a view to providing death and disability cover  to rural landless households, the 'Aam Aadmi Bima 
Yojana' (AABY) has been launched on 2nd October, 20 07. Under the scheme, the head of the family or one  
earning member in the family will be insured. The Central Government will bear 50% of the premium of Rs. 200/- 
per year per person and the remaining 50% of the premium will be borne by State Government. The benefits under 
the scheme include Rs. 30,000/- in case of natural death; Rs. 75,000/- in case of death due to acciden t or total 
permanent disability due to accident. In case of partial disability due to accident, the insurance cover would be Rs. 
37,500/-. The children of beneficiaries of AABY stu dying in classes 9th to 12th standard are eligible to a 
scholarship @Rs. 300/- per quarter per child.  
Similarly, under the National Old Age Pension Scheme, all persons above the age of 65 years who belong to the 
household below the poverty line according to the criterion prescribed by Government of India are eligible for old 
age pension.

Number of child labour identified  
1354. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of LABOUR  AND EMPLOYMENT be 
pleased to state:  
 what, is the total number of child labour which has  been identified in the country during the last thr ee 
years, State-wise; 
 how many people indulging in using children for various labours in the country have been brought to book; 
 whether the children so identified have been rehabilitated or not; 
 whether Government is using any revised mechanism to identify the child misuse in the country and if so, 
the details thereof; and 
 whether Government intends to bring in severe punishment to the offenders and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND  EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR 
FERNANDES): (a) The estimation of the number of child labour in the country State-wise, is done on the basis of 
the census carried out by the Registrar General of India once in every ten years. The last such Census  was carried 
out in 2001. Therefore, yearly data regarding existence of child labour State-wise is not maintained.  
(b) and (c) The Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986 prohibits employment of children below the 
age of 14 years in 15 Occupations and 57 Processes.  State Governments are the appropriate authority fo r the 
implementation of the provisions of the Act for the areas coming under their jurisdiction. As per the information 
received from the State Governments, prosecutions launched and convictions obtained were 77,617 and 22 ,657 
respectively since 1997-98 to 2006-07. The children withdrawn from work are rehabilitated under the National Child 
Labour Scheme being implemented by the Government.  
 No, Sir. 
 There are adequate provisions available under the existing Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 
1986. As per Section 14 of the Act, any person who employs a child in any occupation or process where 
employment of children is banned under the Act, is liable for punishment with imprisonment for a term which 
shall not be less than 3 months but which extend to  one year and or with fine ranging from Rs. 10,000/ - to Rs. 
20,000/-.

Unemployment in agricultural and handloom workers  
1359. SHRI PENUMALLI MADHU: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 whether Government is aware that unemployment in agricultural labour and loss of livelihood among 
handloom workers has risen glaringly; and 
 if so, what are the steps contemplated by Government to increase employment in the two sectors? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT (SHRIMATI 
SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) As per the 2001 Census report, the number of agricultural labourers has 
increased from 8.60 crore to 10.68 crore as compared to 1991 Census. With regard to the handloom secto r, it 
provides employment to about 65 lakh handloom weavers and allied workers. In order to sustain the employment of 
weavers in Handloom Sector, the Government of India has introduced Integrated Handloom Development 
Scheme, Marketing and Export Promotion Scheme, Handloom Weavers Comprehensive Welfare Scheme, Mill 
Gate Price Scheme and Diversified Handloom Development Scheme to be implemented during the Eleventh Five 
Year Plan. These schemes will enable the handloom weavers to enhance production, productivity and efficiency of the 
handloom sector and enhance their income and socio-economic status by upgrading then-skills and providing 
infrastructural input and marketing support. Further, to increase employment opportunities in rural areas, the 
Ministry of Rural Development through State Governments and Union Territory Administrations implements a 
number of Centrally  

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    151  
Sponsored Schemes for employment generation for people living in rural areas of the country. The programmes are 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) for self employment, Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) 
and National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) for wage employment.  
To provide more self employment opportunities to the BPL families, including handloom workers the SGSY is 
already being implemented in all the districts of the country which covers all aspects of self employment such as 
organization of poor in self help groups and their capacity building training, selection of activities , technology 
and marketing support etc. Similarly for willing rural households including agricultural workers, the National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) 2005 is presently being implemented in 330 districts of the country a nd 
would be extended to the remaining districts w.e.f. 1st  April, 2008. The objective of NREGA is to ensure that local 
employment is provided to every willing rural household for at least 100 days in a financial year and the process of 
employment generation is used for building durable asserts, strengthening of livelihood resource based of rural poor.

Generation of employment under NREGA  
1370. SHRI P.R. RAJAN: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 whether the NREGA has generated sufficient employment; 
 if so, the details thereof including the number of days of employment generated, employment provided 
to women, grant allotted to States and total grant utilized for the last one year State-wise; 

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    161  
 the details of complaints in delay in providing wages and measure taken lo rectify it, if any; and 
 the details of the specific wage pattern and facilities at the work site? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR 
SAHU): (a) Yes, Sir. National Rural Employment Guar antee Act provides for a legal guarantee for 100 da ys of 
employment in every financial year to every rural household for doing unskilled manual work on demand. The Act was 
implemented in 200 districts with effect from 2.2.2006. During 2006-07, NREGA as a wage employment programme has 
been able to generate 90.5 crore person days of employment in 200 districts. 130 additional districts were covered under 
the Act from 1.4.07 and during 2007-08 (upto January, 2008) 100.30 crore person days of employment has been generated. 
Further, during 2006-07, 2.10 crore households were provided employment. During the current financial year (upto January, 
2008), 2.82 crore households have demanded employment out of which 2.80 crore have been provided employment.  
 The requisite details is enclosed as Statement-I (See below). 
 NREG Act provides that the disbursement of daily wages shall be made on a weekly basis or in any case not later 
than a fortnight after the date on which such work was done. The Act further provides that in case the payment of wages is not 
made within the specified period, the labourers shall be entitled to receive payment of compensation as per the provisions of 
the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 (4 to 1936). It is for the State Governments to ensure prompt and fair payment of wages 
to all labourers employed under a programme of the scheme. As such, as and when any complaint is received regarding 
delay in payment of wages, it is referred to the concerned State Government for taking corrective measures. 
 NREGA provides for workers entitlements during the course of work. These include medical treatment (including 
hospitalization) at government cost for injured workers for the injury acquired while working, ex-gratia payment to the legal 
heirs of the deceased or permanently disabled workers by accident arising out of and in the course of employment, safe drinking 
water, shade for children and periods of rest, first aid box and creche facility for children below 6 years of age of the female 
NREGA workers. A Statement containing State-wise details of the prevailing wages, applicable to NREGA, is enclosed 
as Statement - II.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT (SHRIMATI 
SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) Under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), as per programme guidelines, the 
first instalment amounting to 50% of the cleared value of projects or annual allocation whichever is lower is released 
subject to fulfilment of conditions, if any, stipulated earlier. The release of 2nd instalment is subject to utilisation of 
60% of the available funds and completion of at least 80% of the road works awarded in the year previous to the 
proceeding year and 100% of the awarded works of all the years preceding that year, and fulfilment of other conditions, 
if any, stipulated while releasing the previous instalment. The release of the second instalment in a year is also 
subject to submission of Utilisation Certificate for the funds released earlier, year-wise in the form prescribed, 
Certificate by the Bank Manager indicating the balance amount on date of issue of the Certificate and the interest 
credited, Certificate regarding the requisite physical completion of works, Audited Statement of Accounts etc. For 
ensuring high level of quality in works PMGSY programme guidelines have the provision for three tier Quality Control 
Mechanism. The first two tiers of the Quality Control Structure are overseen by the State Quality Coordinators, 
appointed by the State Governments. The first tier of quality control mechanism is in-house quality control at the level of 
executing agencies. The field laboratories are established by the Contractors and mandatory tests on the quality of 
material and workmanship are conducted under the supervision of Programme Implementation Units (PIUs). Quality 
Control Handbooks have been prescribed and test records are maintained by the PIUs in the prescribed Quality Control 
registers. The second tier provides for quality monitoring by the State Governments through independent State Quality 
Monitors (SQMs). SQMs are deployed to ensure that quality issues are properly being attended to at the first tier, The* 
third tier of this arrangement consists of quality monitoring of works through random inspection by independent 
National Quality Monitors (NQMs).  
(b) Details of works inspected by independent National Quality Monitors in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka,

(PIUs) immediately after inspection for taking appropriate action. The action taken reports (ATRs) are prepared 
by the PIUs and sent to the National Rural Roads De velopment Agency (NRRDA) through State Quality 
Coordinator. If defects in the work are rectified and the action of rectification is verified by independent quality 
monitors in the subsequent inspections, the 'Unsatisfactory' grading of the work is improved to 'Satisfactory' 
grading. NRRDA monitors the submission of ATRs and States are appraised of the status of ATRs during various 
meetings etc. The State Governments are to take app ropriate action against the concerned officers and the 
contractors, if the defects observed by Quality Monitors are of non-rectifiable nature. Physical and Financial progress 
of works taken up under PMGSY is also regularly reviewed for ensuring proper implementation of the programme.

Efforts to promote research in Nano technology  
tl384. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: Will the Minister of  SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased 
to state:  
 whether it is a fact that there is not enough research activity in Nano technology; 
 if so, the efforts being made to promote research activities; 
 whether cooperation is being sought at international level in this regard; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Several scientists from 
various scientific institutions and universities ar ound the country are very actively involved in rese arch and 
development in nano-science and nano-technology. Various Ministries/Departments of Government of India such as 
the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Dep artment of Information Technology (DIT), Defence 
Research and Development Organization (DRDO), Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Department 
of Biotechnology (DBT) have been supporting R&D in Nano Science and Technology. DST launched a special  
Nano Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI) in Oc tober, 2001. The NSTI had focused on research and 
development in nano-science and technology in a com prehensive manner so that India can become a signif icant 
player in the area and contribute to the development of new technologies besides carrying out basic research at the 
frontiers of knowledge. The programme supported R&D  projects, strengthening of characterization and 
infrastructural facilities, creation of centres of excellence, generation of trained manpower, joint projects between 
educational institutions and industry for technology development etc.  
While very good and internationally competitive fun damental studies are being carried out on nanoscale  
systems, India has to catch up in the area of Nano- technology. The Government has launched a Mission t o 
encourage research work in the field of Nano Science and Technology with an allocation Rs. 1000 crore for 5 
years. It is planned to launch a variety of educati onal and HRD programmes, R&D programmes, establish 
centres of excellence, promote institution-industry linked projects through increased public private p artnerships, 
promote entrepreneurship through establishment of b usiness incubators, etc. as part of the Nano Missio n. The 
Nano Mission also plans to put in special efforts t owards development and commercialization of Nano-
Technology, not only through public private partnerships but also by encouraging and enabling the private sector to 
invest in, and leverage, this sunrise technology. There are also plans to establish three major Instit utes of Nano 
Science and Technology in the country.  
(c) and (d) A number of countries including United States of America, Brazil, Canada, Japan, Germany, 
Swedan, Swiss, Taiwan and European Commission have sought cooperation

Written Answers to  [12 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    179  
(c) if so, to what extent the strategy has been helpful in improving the conditions of the cotton growers in the 
Vidarbha Region in Maharashtra?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES ( SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to 
(c) The Government of India launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC) in February, 2000 in Ninth Five 
Year Plan, with the objective of improvement in the production, productivity and quality of cotton and reduction in 
cost of cultivation, in order to provide abundant supply of good quality cotton at competitive prices to the textile 
industry and a remunerative return to the farmers. The scheme is functional in Maharashtra State also including 
Vidarbha region. The mission consists of four mini missions, which are being jointly implemented by the Ministry 
of Agriculture and the Ministry of Textiles. Objectives of Mini Missions (MMs) are as under:  
(i) Mini Mission I relates to Research and Development on cotton, which strengthen especially on genetic 
improvement of cotton, cottonseed technology, Resource management for quality cotton production, 
modernization of cotton cultivation, and post harvest technology. This scheme is being implementing 
by the Indian Council for Agriculture Research (ICAR).  
(ii) Mini Mission II relates to Dissemination of te chnology to farmers. The main components include 
production and supply of certified seed of varietie s/hybrids, transfer of technology through field 
demonstration & farmers' training and thereby increasing production and productivity of cotton. The 
Ministry of Agriculture implements mini mission-II. 
(iii) Mini Mission III relates to improvement in marketing infrastructure and includes the revival of dormant 
market yards, improvement in existing market yards and setting up of new market yards.  
(iv) Mini Mission IV arms at modernization of ginning and pressing factories and thereby improving the quality 
of cotton by reducing contamination ensuring better prices to the growers.  
(Ministry of Textiles is the nodal agency for MM-III & MM-IV of TMC which are being implemented through 
Cotton Corporation of India Ltd., Mumbai)

Repealing JPM Act  
1395. SHRI PRAVEEN RASHTRAPAL: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state:  
 whether Government is aware that since the enactment of Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory use in 
Packing Commodities) Act, 1987, Government is imposing absolute reservation for jute packaging for foodgrain 
and sugar instead of diluting the same; 
 whether Government is also aware that the import of jute bags is increasing in case of shortage of jute in the 
country after the decision taken by Government to reserve 100 per cent of foodgrain and sugar to be packaged in 
jute packing material; and 
 whether Government is considering to repeal the JPM Act, 1987? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI E.V.K.S.  
ELANGOVAN): (a) Government has not imposed absolute reservation for packaging for  
foodgrains and sugar since enactment of Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory use in Packing  
Commodities) Act, 1987. The reservation was diluted in the years 2000,2001, 2002,2003,  
2004 & 2005 for sugar and in the years 2000, 2001, 2002 and 2004 for foodgrain. Beside  
that, the order issued under JPM Act, 1987 provides that in case of shortage or disruption of  
supply of jute packaging material, Ministry of Textiles may in consultation with the user  
Ministries concerned relax the provisions upto a maximum of 20% for foodgrains and sugar 
respectively.  
 
 There is no co-relation between import of jute bags  and provisions under JPM Act because use of 
imported jute bags for packing foodgrains and sugar under JPM Act, 1987, is not permissible. 
 No, Sir.
